edits.fix: Use the standard footer with an id on every page, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / K1-1", in place of a bare page number at the right margin.

edits.quote: Blocks must fit inside the thick line and sit on the thin lines.
edits.fix: "Sit on the thin lines" does not say that block edges must follow the grid. Use the wording from the other bands: "Each block must cover whole small triangles inside the thick line."

edits.quote: Find all the ways to cover each shape with blue blocks. Put each way on a shape of its own.
edits.fix: Say whether a turned or flipped copy of a covering counts as a new way. The small hexagon has 2 coverings that are mirror images, and the long hexagon has 3. There are 3 and 4 shapes, so the spare shapes may also make a K-1 child think a way is missing. Add "A turned or flipped copy counts as a new way. You may not need every shape." Use the same wording in P6 (6 ways, 8 shapes).

edits.quote: Page 7: four hexagon boards under the header with no problem line
edits.fix: Label the page as a continuation of Problem 6 so the child or the parent volunteer knows these boards belong to P6.

k-1.summary: A strong K-1 sheet. Children meet impossible boards (including the 8-triangle trapezoid, which has 5 up and 3 down triangles), fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 (answers 2, 3, 4), finding every covering (2, 3 and 6 ways), fewest blocks (3, 3, 4, where three trapezoids beat the hexagon on the side-3 triangle) and a placement game (first, second, first, first, second). All of it is correct, uses actual-size boards and has recording boxes. Only small wording fixes are needed: whether turned coverings count as new ways, the footer, and the unlabeled overflow page.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer with an id, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / G23-1", on all pages.

edits.quote: Imagine a triangle board with 10 small triangles along each side.
edits.fix: A child can count every triangle in the bottom row (9 on the side-5 triangle), so "along each side" is ambiguous. Tie it to P3: "a triangle board like the ones in Problem 3, but with 10 small triangles along each side (the biggest one in Problem 3 has 5)."

grades-2-3.summary: This band develops kernel 1 well. Possible and impossible boards contrast an odd board, an even board with 7 up and 5 down triangles, a forced star, holes of the same colour, holes of opposite colours, and a balanced bowtie that still fails. Fewest greens follow (2-5, then 10 and 100), then chevrons (4, 5, 4, 5, never better than blue), an invented 20-triangle board, and the two-hole rule (I checked all 276 pairs: exactly the up/down pairs work). The mathematics is correct and the boards are actual size. Only a footer change and one ambiguous phrase need fixing.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer with an id, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / G45-1", on all pages.

edits.quote: Find all the different ways to do it
edits.fix: The board has symmetry, so say that turned or flipped copies count as different coverings (6 in all). The ribbon count in P5 and the answers to P7 and P8 (20 each) depend on this.

edits.quote: On the small boards below, draw all your coverings from Problem 1 again.
edits.fix: Redrawing six coverings is copying, not thinking, and the fixed 2x4 grid of boards does not let children arrange the graph. Have them number their P1 drawings and draw the flip graph as numbered dots joined by lines, and keep a few spare boards.

edits.quote: Then find the fewest flips that change covering E into covering F in Problem 3, and explain why nobody can do it with fewer.
edits.fix: The E-to-F count (8) was already asked for in P3's box. Rewrite as "Then explain why nobody can change covering E into covering F with fewer flips than your answer in Problem 3."

edits.quote: A full page of 15 ruled lines with no diagram
edits.fix: Swap about half the lines for two small hexagon boards, or space to write the ribbons of E (RRLL, RRLL) and F (LLRR, LLRR), so children can work out the argument on the page.

edits.quote: Draw them on the small hexagons below (25 hexagons about 1.2 in wide, triangle edge about 0.3 in)
edits.fix: Drawing 12 rhombi on 0.3-inch triangles twenty times is fiddly and mostly copying. Let children record each covering by its pair of ribbons (keep a few boards for sketching), or use fewer, larger boards.

grades-4-5.summary: This band develops kernel 2 through a well-chosen sequence: the 6 coverings of the (1,2,2) hexagon, its flip graph (diameter 4), flip distances on the side-2 hexagon (A to B is 3, C to D is 4, E to F is 8, all verified), 4-flip round trips and why odd ones fail, ribbons with a correct worked example (LRRLR), the parity proof, and counts of 20 for both the (1,3,3) and side-2 hexagons. All diagrams and claims check out. The edits are about recording load (redrawing, tiny boards, a page of lines) and one repeated question.

overall.strongest: Grades 2-3 is the strongest band: a tight, correct sequence of contrasting boards that leads children from trying coverings to the up/down counting argument, its generalization, and inventing their own hard board.
overall.weakest: The weakest point is the grades 4-5 recording load: recopying the P1 coverings, a page of bare lines in P6, and twenty drawings on tiny P8 hexagons, which use up time without adding thinking.
